# Applying the DE Pipeline to the Placenta Dataset to Determine Sex Differences in Gene Expression

This pipeline is adapted from the limma workflow vignette on Bioconductor:
https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/workflows/vignettes/RNAseq123/inst/doc/limmaWorkflow.html

```{r ReportingOptions, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
options(width = 60) # Limits output to 60 characters
```

# Load packages

Install the necessary packages for our analysis.  The function 'require' returns a true value if it is already installed, so if it is not, we need to install before loading

```{r Packages, warning=FALSE}

library(gplots)
library(ggplot2)
library(limma)
library(ggpubr)
library(edgeR)
library(Polychrome)
library(RColorBrewer)
library(EnhancedVolcano)
library(pheatmap)
library(variancePartition)
library(matrixStats)
library(stringr)

```

# Set working directory

Your working directory is where all your output files are going to be saved.

``` {r WorkingDirectory, tidy=TRUE, tidy.opts=list(width.cutoff=60)}
# you will need to change this to the directory you are working in
# make sure to include the / at the end of the directory path

input_directory = "C:/Users/plaisiersb/OneDrive - National Institutes of Health/Documents/Projects/Placenta/HG38/"

output_directory = "C:/Users/plaisiersb/OneDrive - National Institutes of Health/Documents/Projects/Placenta/HG38/Correct_BatchCovariate/"

output_file_tag = "model2"

```

# Read in placenta data
Read in datasets containing genesID, phenotypes, and genecounts. We will be using DGElists for organizing information.

```{r DataSetup, tidy=TRUE, tidy.opts=list(width.cutoff=60)}
# Save imported data as variables
pheno <- read.delim(paste0(input_directory,"pheno_batch1and2.csv"), header=TRUE, sep=",", check.names = FALSE)
counts <- read.delim(paste0(input_directory,"geneCounts_batch1and2_Cont09rerun.csv"), header=TRUE, sep=",", check.names = FALSE)

# change batch to not be numeric so R doesn't get confused
pheno$batch = ifelse(pheno$batch == 1, "one","two")

check_counts = colnames(counts)[2:length(counts)]
check_pheno = pheno$sample
check_counts == check_pheno
if (! all (check_counts == check_pheno)) {
  stop("pheno file has to have the same sample order as counts")
}

# set row names with a unique version of those gene names
row.names(counts)=make.unique(counts$Geneid) 
counts[1] = NULL  # remove gene name column so that you can work with the data
dim(counts) # check out how much you have in your counts file

# using these to set which conditions we want
# move output to a new folder to indicate which conditions were used
filter_female = FALSE # if we want to filter for females only
filter_male = FALSE # if we want to filter for males only
filter_hyp = FALSE # if we want to filter for hypertensive only
filter_norm = FALSE # if we want to filter for normotensive only

if(filter_female == TRUE) {
  indices = which(grepl("female",pheno$sex)==TRUE)
  pheno = pheno[pheno$sex == "female",]
}
if(filter_male == TRUE) {
  indices = which(pheno$sex == "male")
  pheno = pheno[pheno$sex == "male",]
}
if (filter_female | filter_male) {
  counts <- counts[indices]
}

if(filter_hyp == TRUE) {
  indices = which(grepl("hyp",pheno$case_control)==TRUE)
  pheno = pheno[pheno$case_control == "hyp",]
}
if(filter_norm == TRUE) {
  indices = which(pheno$case_control=="norm")
  pheno = pheno[pheno$case_control == "norm",]
}
if (filter_hyp | filter_norm) {
  counts <- counts[indices]
}


```

```{r DGEList, tidy=TRUE, tidy.opts=list(width.cutoff=60)}

# Create a new DGElist object

if (filter_female == TRUE | filter_male == TRUE) {
  # Normotensive vs hypertensive analysis
  x = DGEList(counts = counts, lib.size = colSums(counts), norm.factors = rep(1,ncol(counts)), samples = colnames(counts), group = pheno$case_control, genes = row.names(counts), remove.zeros = TRUE)
  group = as.factor(pheno$case_control)
  x$sex_casecontrol = as.factor(pheno$case_control)

  } else if ( filter_norm == TRUE | filter_hyp == TRUE) {
  # Male vs Female analysis
   x = DGEList(counts = counts, lib.size = colSums(counts), norm.factors = rep(1,ncol(counts)), samples = colnames(counts), group = pheno$sex, genes = row.names(counts), remove.zeros = TRUE)
  group = as.factor(pheno$sex)
  x$sex_casecontrol <- as.factor(pheno$sex)
  } else {
  x = DGEList(counts = counts, lib.size = colSums(counts), norm.factors = rep(1,ncol(counts)), samples = colnames(counts), group = NULL, genes = row.names(counts), remove.zeros = TRUE)
  
  }
dim(x) # show how much is left after removing all-zero rows

samplenames = colnames(x) #save sample names for plotting below

x$batch = as.factor(pheno$batch)
x$placenta = as.factor(pheno$sample_id)
x$sex = as.factor(pheno$sex)
x$case_control = as.factor(pheno$case_control)

```

# Data Preprocessing
For differential expression and related analyses, gene expression is rarely considered at the level of raw counts since libraries sequenced at a greater depth will result in higher counts. Rather, it is common practice to transform raw counts onto a scale that accounts for such library size differences. Popular transformations include counts per million (CPM), log2-counts per million (log-CPM), reads per kilobase of transcript per million (RPKM), and fragments per kilobase of transcript per million (FPKM).

Here raw counts are converted to CPM and log-CPM values using the cpm function in edgeR. RPKM values are just as easily calculated as CPM values using the rpkm function in edgeR if gene lengths are available.

CPM values adjust for the fact that some genes were sequenced more than others. A CPM value of 1 for a gene equates to having 20 counts in the sample with the lowest sequencing depth or 76 counts in the sample with the greatest sequencing depth 

When the parameter 'log' is set to 'TRUE', the cpm function adds an offset to the CPM values before converting to the log2-scale. By default, the offset is 2/L where 2 is the “prior count” and L is the average library size in millions, so the log-CPM values are related to the CPM values by log2(CPM + 2/L). This calculation ensures that any two read counts with identical CPM values will also have identical log-CPM values. 

```{r Preprocessing, tidy=TRUE, tidy.opts=list(width.cutoff=60)}

# calculate the mean and median of the counts
#  (we multiply by 1e-6 to represent the mean and median in millions)
L <- mean(x$samples$lib.size) * 1e-6
M <- median(x$samples$lib.size) * 1e-6
c(L, M)  # see what the mean and median are

```

# Removing genes that are lowly expressed 
All datasets will include a mix of genes that are expressed and those that are not expressed. Whilst it is of interest to examine genes that are expressed in one condition but not in another, some genes are unexpressed throughout all samples.

Genes that do not have a worthwhile number of reads in any sample should be filtered out of the downstream analyses. There are several reasons for this. From a biological point of view, genes that not expressed at a biologically meaningful level in any condition are not of interest and are therefore best ignored. From a statistical point of view, removing low count genes allows the mean-variance relationship in the data to be estimated with greater reliability and also reduces the number of statistical tests that need to be carried out in downstream analyses looking at differential expression.


```{r FilterLowExpression, tidy=TRUE, tidy.opts=list(width.cutoff=60)}

# filter genes using the filterByExpr function in edgeR
if (filter_male | filter_female | filter_norm | filter_hyp) {
  keep.exprs <- filterByExpr(x, group=group)
} else {
  keep.exprs <- filterByExpr(x, group=NULL)
}
x <- x[keep.exprs,, keep.lib.sizes=FALSE]
dim(x) # see how much remains after filtering out low expression genes

```

# Normalising gene expression distributions
During the sample preparation or sequencing process, external factors that are not of biological interest can affect the expression of individual samples. For example, samples processed in the first batch of an experiment can have higher expression overall when compared to samples processed in a second batch. It is assumed that all samples should have a similar range and distribution of expression values. Any plot showing the per sample expression distributions, such as a density or boxplot, is useful in determining whether any samples are dissimilar to others. 

Normalisation is required to ensure that the expression distributions of each sample are similar across the entire experiment. Normalisation by the method of trimmed mean of M-values (TMM) (Robinson and Oshlack 2010) is performed using the calcNormFactors function in edgeR. The normalisation factors calculated here are used as a scaling factor for the library sizes. When working with DGEList-objects, these normalisation factors are automatically stored in x$samples$norm.factors. For this dataset the effect of TMM-normalisation is mild, as evident in the magnitude of the scaling factors, which are all relatively close to 1.

```{r Normalization, tidy=TRUE, tidy.opts=list(width.cutoff=60), fig.height=8}
# use calcNormFactors function to calculate how much you want to multiply by to make sure the data are in comparable range to one another
x_norm <- calcNormFactors(x, method = "TMM")
x_norm$samples$norm.factors

lcpm_norm = edgeR::cpm(x_norm, log = TRUE)

# if (filter_male == TRUE) {
#   write.csv(lcpm_norm, file = paste0(output_directory,"lcpm_male_",output_file_tag,".csv"))
# } else if (filter_female == TRUE) {
#   write.csv(lcpm_norm, file = paste0(output_directory,"lcpm_female_",output_file_tag,".csv"))
# } else if (filter_norm == TRUE) {
#   write.csv(lcpm_norm, file = paste0(output_directory,"lcpm_norm_",output_file_tag,".csv"))
# } else if (filter_hyp == TRUE) {
#   write.csv(lcpm_norm, file = paste0(output_directory,"lcpm_hyp_",output_file_tag,".csv"))
# } else {
#   write.csv(lcpm_norm, file = paste0(output_directory,"lcpm_all_",output_file_tag,".csv"))
# }

# MDS plot
group = as.factor(pheno$sex_casecontrol)
design = model.matrix(~group)
expr_bc = removeBatchEffect(x_norm, batch = pheno$batch, design = design)

group_colors = c(
  male_norm   = "lightblue",
  male_hyp = "blue",
  female_norm = "gold",
  female_hyp = "orange"
)
cols = group_colors[pheno$sex_casecontrol]
plotMDS(x_norm, top = 1000, col = cols, pch = 16)

# PCA plot
pca = prcomp(t(expr_bc), scale. = TRUE)
plot(pca$x[,1],pca$x[,2], col = cols, pch = 19)

```

# Differential Expression Analysis

In order to use linear modeling to determine which genes are differentially expressed, we first set up a design matrix relating our samples to our variable of interest (sex) and contrasts to make the comparisons we are interested in (female vs male, male vs female).

In limma, linear modelling is carried out on the log-CPM values which are assumed to be normally distributed and the mean-variance relationship is accommodated using precision weights calculated by the voom function. When operating on a DGEList-object, voom converts raw counts to log-CPM values by automatically extracting library sizes and normalization factors from x itself. 

Since we are analyzing data with four samples for each placenta, we are using the DREAM versions of these limma functions designed for this purpose.  This is explained in this vignette: 
https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/variancePartition/inst/doc/dream.html


```{r DesignMatrixContrasts, eval=TRUE, tidy=TRUE, tidy.opts=list(width.cutoff=60)}

# The variable to be tested must be a fixed effect
# Meaning that we have to be using discrete groupings of samples
#   sex (male vs female) or case_control (norm vs hyp) is the variable we are interested in
#   sample_id is the variable we are accounting for, the id for the placenta
if (filter_female == TRUE | filter_male == TRUE) {
  form = ~ case_control + batch + (1 | sample_id)
} else if (filter_hyp == TRUE | filter_norm == TRUE) {
  form = ~ sex + batch + (1 | sample_id)
} else {
  form = ~ sex * case_control + (1 | batch) + (1 | sample_id)
}

# estimate weights using linear mixed model of dream
rownames(pheno) = pheno$sample
v = voomWithDreamWeights(x_norm, form, pheno)

# Fit the dream model on each gene
# For the hypothesis testing, by default,
# dream() uses the KR method for <= 20 samples,
# otherwise it uses the Satterthwaite approximation
fitmm = dream(v, form, pheno)
fitmm <- eBayes(fitmm)

# take a look at the top results
head(fitmm$design, 3)

# print out the full results table for further analysis
if (filter_female == TRUE | filter_male == TRUE) {
  results = topTable(fitmm, coef = "case_controlnorm", n=Inf)
} else if (filter_hyp == TRUE | filter_norm == TRUE) {
  if ("sexfemale" %in% colnames(fitmm$design)) {
    results = topTable(fitmm, coef = "sexfemale", n=Inf)
  } else if ("sexmale" %in% colnames(fitmm$design)) {
    results = topTable(fitmm, coef = "sexmale", n=Inf)
  }
} else {
  results = topTable(fitmm, coef = "case_controlnorm", n=Inf)
}

if (filter_male == TRUE) {
  write.csv(results, file = paste0(output_directory,"dream_diffexpr_male_hypnorm_",output_file_tag,".csv"))
} else if (filter_female == TRUE) {
  write.csv(results, file = paste0(output_directory,"dream_diffexpr_female_hypnorm_",output_file_tag,".csv"))
} else if (filter_norm == TRUE) {
  write.csv(results, file = paste0(output_directory,"dream_diffexpr_norm_femalemale_",output_file_tag,".csv"))
} else if (filter_hyp == TRUE) {
  write.csv(results, file = paste0(output_directory,"dream_diffexpr_hyp_femalemale_",output_file_tag,".csv"))
} else {
  write.csv(results, file = paste0(output_directory,"dream_diffexpr_hypnorm_all",output_file_tag,".csv"))
}


```

# Volcano plot

A volcano plot shows log fold change on the x-axis and log p-value on the y axis. Log fold change is given a positive sign if average expression in females is higher or negative if average expression in males is higher. This brings genes that are significantly differentially expressed away from both axes.  The EnhancedVolcano function shown here does a lot of labeling and coloring automatically, which is pleasing to the eye and very convenient for making figures for papers and presentations.

``` {r VolcanoPlot, eval=TRUE, tidy=TRUE, tidy.opts=list(width.cutoff=60), fig.height=8}

# volcano plot
EnhancedVolcano(results, lab = results$genes, x = 'logFC', y = 'adj.P.Val',labSize=3, FCcutoff = 0.3, pCutoff = 0.05, drawConnectors = TRUE)

EnhancedVolcano(results, lab = results$genes, x = 'logFC', y = 'P.Value',labSize=3, FCcutoff = 0.3, pCutoff = 0.05, drawConnectors = TRUE)

length(results$genes[results$P.Value < 0.05])


if (filter_male == TRUE) {
  EnhancedVolcano(results, lab = results$genes, x = 'logFC', y = 'P.Value',labSize=3, FCcutoff = 0.3, pCutoff = 0.05, drawConnectors = TRUE)
  ggsave(paste0(output_directory,"dream_volcano_male_hypnorm_",output_file_tag,".pdf"), height = 8, width = 8)
} 
if (filter_female == TRUE) {
  EnhancedVolcano(results, lab = results$genes, x = 'logFC', y = 'P.Value',labSize=3, FCcutoff = 0.3, pCutoff = 0.05, drawConnectors = TRUE)
  ggsave(paste0(output_directory,"dream_volcano_female_hypnorm_",output_file_tag,".pdf"), height = 8, width = 8)
} 
if (filter_norm == TRUE) {
  EnhancedVolcano(results, lab = results$genes, x = 'logFC', y = 'P.Value',labSize=3, FCcutoff = 0.3, pCutoff = 0.05, drawConnectors = TRUE)
  ggsave(paste0(output_directory,"dream_volcano_norm_femalemale_",output_file_tag,".pdf"), height = 8, width = 8)
} 
if (filter_hyp == TRUE) {
  EnhancedVolcano(results, lab = results$genes, x = 'logFC', y = 'P.Value',labSize=3, FCcutoff = 0.3, pCutoff = 0.05, drawConnectors = TRUE)
  ggsave(paste0(output_directory,"dream_volcano_hyp_femalemale_",output_file_tag,".pdf"), height = 8, width = 8)
} 


```

# Plot gene of interest

```{r eval=FALSE}

gene_of_interest = c("NPIPA5")

lcpm_norm = data.frame(edgeR::cpm(x_norm, log=TRUE))
write.csv(lcpm_norm, paste0(output_directory,"lcpm_norm_batchcorrected.csv"))

gene_lcpm_norm = data.frame(t(lcpm_norm[rownames(lcpm_norm) %in% gene_of_interest,]))
colnames(gene_lcpm_norm) = c("gene")
gene_lcpm_norm$sex = ifelse(grepl("XY",rownames(gene_lcpm_norm), fixed = TRUE),"male","female")
gene_lcpm_norm$status = ifelse(grepl("Cont",rownames(gene_lcpm_norm), fixed = TRUE),"normotensive","hypertensive")
gene_lcpm_norm$placenta = str_split(rownames(gene_lcpm_norm), "_", simplify = TRUE)[, 1]
gene_lcpm_norm$quadrant = str_split(rownames(gene_lcpm_norm), "_", simplify = TRUE)[, 2]

ggplot(gene_lcpm_norm, aes(x = placenta, y = gene, fill = status)) +
  geom_boxplot() + 
  geom_point() +
  ggtitle(gene_of_interest) +
  theme_minimal()

```
